trace.goal: Teach one concrete operator lesson with specific examples and conviction.
expected_facts: The answer should explain that public multiples matter because they shape private funding expectations and exit math.
It should distinguish between what founders can control and what they cannot.
It should advise founders to focus on fundamentals rather than obsessing over market chatter.
rubric_must_haves: Provides practical founder guidance, not just investor commentary.
Includes at least one example of how multiples affect fundraising, burn, or planning.
trace.gold_reference: A strong answer should say that founders cannot ignore public multiples because they influence valuation, fundraising, and investor psychology, but they also should not let them run the company. The right move is to understand the implications, tighten execution, and build the kind of business that works under tougher market assumptions.

trace.answer: So you've heard this on Twitter, you've seen it everywhere in private conversations, we're talking about the state of public multiples right now. And I think what worries me and should worry every founder out there is how much your investors care. They really do. They obsess over multiples. It's one thing they know well when it comes to their funds. When your VC fund raises money, they get paid two percent fees for each year their investments go up in value. So if your start-up goes up in value, your VC gets more money. If it doesn't go up in value, your VC makes less money. This is why everyone cares so much about valuations and multiples. But beyond just making them more money, here's where the real anxiety kicks in—when those same investments sell. Let's say it takes five years to make something good enough to attract an acquirer. That means three years before an exit. The time between investment and acquisition is too long for many folks. How does it work? Let's take some examples. What happens to revenue multiples in different scenarios? Well, let's look at Salesforce. Salesforce was acquired by Marc Benioff. It wasn't sold. He bought his company back for $27 billion and then turned around and sold it again. Now let's look at the first time it got sold. At the IPO in 2004, Salesforce had $400 million in revenue. In today's dollars adjusted for inflation, that would have been worth almost $600 million. Now it traded at four times revenue. Today, if it were trading at four times revenue at $500 million in revenue, it'd be worth two billion dollars. That IPO price was actually pretty high. But let's fast forward to 2019. Salesforce went public in '04, but in '19, they were doing $15 billion in revenue with very similar margins. So basically twice the revenue of their IPO. The multiple came down significantly, and yet they grew tenfold.
